terms.gloss: of the mind (as against the body)
terms.grammar: genitive of animus, after the noun
evidence: Cic. Sen. 38: eās rēs tueor animī nōn corporis vīribus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says “of the mind” with the genitive, usually set against corporis (see mind).

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 46: studia doctrīnae (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The plural of studium, eagerness; with a genitive, the pursuit itself: studia doctrīnae, litterārum.

evidence: Apul. Dogm. Plat. 1.3; Aug. Gen. ad Lit. 12.7 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A word of late philosophy, from intellēctus, understanding; the long ē by Lachmann’s law, as in lēctus.

phrases.latin: senibus autem labōrēs corporis minuendī, exercitātiōnēs animī etiam augendae videntur
phrases.english: for the old, bodily labour should be lessened, and exercise of the mind even increased

phrases.latin: eās rēs tueor animī nōn corporis vīribus
phrases.english: I keep up these things with the strength of my mind, not of my body

sources: Lewis & Short: animus · Lewis & Short: studium · Lewis & Short: intellectualis
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
